Maqbul Ahmed, Advocate ------ For the Petitioners. 
Nesar Ahmed with BA Rashid, Advocates ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Chittagong City Corporation, represented by its Mayor and 3 others  ------ Petitioners 
Vs.
Md Afzal Hossain and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
ABM Khairul Haque J : This Rule Nisi was issued at the instance of Chittagong City Corporation and 3 others, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 4-11-2002 (Annexure-A) passed by the Second Labour Court, in Industrial Relations Ordinance Case No. 20 of 2002, should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 2. It appears from the petition that one Md Afzal Hossain, respondent No.2, instituted a case being Industrial Relations Ordinance (IRO) Case No. 20 of 2002, against the petitioner-Corporation, praying for his arrear salary with the direction to work with full pay. After hearing the parties, the Labour Court by its judgment and order dated 4-11-2002, allowed the case on contest and directed the second party-Corporation to withdraw the order of suspension and no allow the first party to resume his duty with his back wages on and from 31-5-1998 within 30 days from the date of the judgment 

 6. It is further stated at paragraph 3 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the Chittagong City Corporation, the petitioner, owns a great number of shops, markets and commercial buildings all over the Chittagong City. It runs its such business establishments by recruiting and employing a huge number of employees and work force and earns a huge profit, as such, the petitioner-Corporation is a commercial establishment. It is further stated in the affidavit that there are 3(three) registered trade unions in the petitioner-Corporation. One of those is known as Chattagram City Corporation Sramik-o-Karmachari League (Registration No. 683) registered with the Registrar of Trade Unions, Chittagong, under the provisions of the Industrial Relations Ordinance. The respondent No. 2 is a member of the said Registered Trade Union and he being a worker filed IRO Case No. 20 of 2002 in the Second Labour Court, Chittagong, under section 34 of the IRO and the Labour Court rightly allowed the case and directed lifting of the order of his suspension and to allow him to resume his duty with back wages on and from 31-5-1998 within a period of 30 days from the date of the judgment. 

 8. Mr Moqbul Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that the IRO Case filed before the Labour Court by the respondent No. 2 was misconceived because the Chittagong City Corporation is neither a commercial establishment nor an industrial enterprise within the meaning of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 or even an establishment under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969, as such, the learned Advocate submits that since the Chittagong City Corporation is not a commercial establishment or an industrial enterprise, the respondent No. 2 does not come within the definition of a worker and is not a worker, rather, he is an employee within the meaning of the Chittagong City Corporation Ordinance, 1977, as such, he did not have any locus standi to file any case under section 34 of the IRO before the Labour Court and the Labour Court erred in law and acted without jurisdiction in disposing of the said case under the provisions of the Labour Laws although the First-Party-Petitioner before the Labour Court, does not come within the definition of the word 'worker.' In support of his contention Mr Moqbul Ahmed, the learned Advocate, refers to the case of Kumudini Hospital vs Kumudini Hospital Karmachari Union and others 43 DLR 655 and also to the case of Chairman, DIT vs Chairman, Second Labour Court 34 DLR (AD) 37. He submits that the respondent No. 2 is an employee and if he is aggrieved by any order of the Corporation, he could file an appeal before the proper authority or might even file a suit before the civil Court but he, not being a worker, did not have any locus standi to file any case either under the provisions of the Industrial Relations Ordinance or even under the provisions of the Standing Orders Act, 1965. 

 9. On the other hand, Mr Nesar Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.2, submits that the respondent No.2 started his career with the petitioner-Corporation initially as an orderly and by dint of his diligence and hard work he was appointed a market inspector, that he joined the service of the Corporation as a worker and remained so even as a market inspector as he was never employed in managerial capacity, as such, according to the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 18 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965, for any misconduct allegedly committed by the respondent No.2, he cannot be kept under suspension beyond the period of 60 days but here in this case he was illegally placed under suspension since 31-5-1998, as such, the order of suspension for this unreasonably long period violated not only the said provision but all canons of law and the Labour Court rightly directed the Corporation to lift the order of suspension and also to make the payment of his arrear salary for the entire period. On the question of maintainability of the case before a Labour Court, the learned Advocate submits that he being a worker within the meaning of the definition given both under the IRO and also under the Act, he has got a right to go before the Labour Court for necessary redress. He further submits that in analysing the definition of the word 'worker' it would appear that the Chittagong City Corporation, established under the Chittagong City Corporation Ordinance, 1982, is a commercial establishment as well as an industrial establishment within the meaning of section 2 of the said Act. He also refers to the definition of the word 'establishment' as appearing in section 2 of the IRO and submits that the Chittagong City Corporation is an 'establishment' and since it is an establishment, it is also an industry, as such, the respondent No.2 is a worker as defined in sub-section xxviii of section 2 of the Ordinance. The learned Advocate finally submits that the respondent No. 2 is a 'worker' because he comes within the definition of worker as appearing in the IRO and since the Chittagong City Corporation also comes within the definition of an 'establishment' he has got the right to go before the Labour Court and the Labour Court justifiably assumes jurisdiction to adjudicate the grievance raised by him against the petitioner-Corporation. In support of his contention Mr Nesar Ahmed, Advocate, firstly refers to the case of State vs Abdul Awal 35 DLR 151 and the case of The Corporation of the City of Nagpur vs Its Employees AIR 1960 (SC) 675 and case of Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board vs A Rajappa AIR 1978 (SC) 548. 

 11. It appears that the respondent No.2 is a market inspector in the Chittagong City Corporation (the 'Corporation' in short). On the allegations of misconduct, disciplinary proceedings were taken against him and he was placed under suspension by an order dated 31-5-1998 (Annexure-X-5). After completion of the enquiry against him a second notice dated 11-1-2000 (Annexure-X-14) was issued to show-cause within 10(ten) days as to why the punishment of removal from the service should not be imposed upon him as he was found guilty in the enquiry report dated 7-11-1999, a copy of which was enclosed with the said notice. The respondent No.2 promptly responded to the said second notice to show cause by his reply dated 18-1-2000 (Annexure-X-16) denying all material allegations and prayed for exonerating him of all allegations, brought against him. But thereafter, no further step was taken in this regard while the order of suspension of the respondent No.2 continued, as such, he filed an IRO case under section 34 of the Ordinance on 10-8-2002, praying for allowing him his arrear salaryand to continue his service with full pay. 

 12. The petitioner-Corporation raised various objections in its written statement, filed on 7-10- 2002 but did not raise the objection with regard to the jurisdiction of the Labour Court in disposing of the said IRO case although it is a settled principle that the objection with regard to jurisdiction of a Court has to be taken at the very outset. This objection was, however, taken in this writ petition. Since the question of jurisdiction of the Court is a question of law we would consider the said point first as to whether the respondent No. 2 is a worker and whether the case under section 34 of the IRO before the Labour Court was at all maintainable. 

 13. The contentions of Mr Nesar Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2, are firstly, the respondent No.2 is not engaged in a supervisory capacity in the Corporation which is a question of fact and not denied by the Corporation in its written statement, as such, deemed to be admitted. Secondly, the Corporation being an industry as defined in sub-section xiv of section 2 of the IRO, it is also an establishment within the meaning of sub-section ix of section 2. Accordingly, the respondent No. 2 is a worker as defined in sub-section xxviii of section 2, As such, his. IRO case before the Labour Court was maintainable. In support of his contentions, the learned Advocate relies on the two decisions of the Supreme Court of India mentioned above. 

 14. In the case of the Corporation of The City of Nag pur vs Its Employees AIR 1960 SC 675, disputes arose between the Corporation and its employees of its various departments with regard to the terms and conditions of their service. On being referred, the State Industrial Court, Nagpur, found that the Corporation was an industry and that on taking evidence, it can be decided whether any department of the Corporation was an industry or not. The Supreme Court of India accepted this legal position of Nagpur Corporation, on the grounds, inter alia, that if a service rendered by an individual or a private person would be an industry, it would equally be an industry in the hands of a Corporation. 

 15. In the case of Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board vs A Rajappa AIR 1978 SC 548 the Supreme Court of India considered the scope of the word "industry' as defined in section G) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947. In explaining the import of the word "industry" Krishna Iyer, Justice held at para-161 : 

 (a) Where a complex of activities, some of which qualify for exemption, others not, involves employees on the total undertaking, some of whom are not 'workmen' as in the University of Delhi case (AIR 1963SC 1873) or some departments are not productive of goods and services if isolated, even then the predominant nature of the services and the integrated nature of the departments as explained in the Corporation of Nagpur (AIR 1960 SC 675) will be the true test. The whole undertaking will be 'industry' although those who are not 'workmen' by definition may not benefit by the status. 

 "Our endeavour in this decision is to provide such working principles. This Court, within a few years of the enactment of the salutary statute, explained the benign sweep of industry in Banerji (AIR 1953 SC 58) which served as beacon in later years Ahmedabad Textile Research (A1R 1961 SC 484) acted on it. Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (A1R 1960 SC 610) and Nagpur Corporation (AIR 1960 SC 675) marched in its sheen. The law shed steady light on industrial inter-relations and the country's tribunals and courts settled down to evolve a progressive labour jurisprudence burying the bad memories of laissez (aire and bitter struggles in this field and nourishing new sprouts of legality fertilised by the seminal ratio in Banerji. Indeed every great judgment is not merely an adjudication of an existing list but an appeal addressed by the present to the emerging future. And here the future responded, harmonising with the humans cape hopefully projected by Part IV of the Constitution. But the drama of a nation's life, especially when it confronts diehard forces, develops situations of imbroglio and tendencies to back-track. And Law quibbles where life wobbles. Judges only read sign and translate symbols in the national sky. So ensued an era of islands of exception dredged up by judicial process .Great clubs were privileged out, liberal professions swam to safety, educational institutions, vast and small, were helped out, diverse charities, disinclined to be charitable to their own weaker workmen, made 'pious pleas and philanthropic appeals to be extricated. A procession of decisions-Solicitor case (AIR 1962 SC 1080), University of Delhi (AIR 1963 SC 1873). Gymkhana Club (AIR 1968 SC 554), Cricket Club of India (AIR 1969 SC 276). Chartered Accountants (1963-1 LLJ 567)): (AIR 1963 Cal) climaxed by Safdarjung (AIR 1970 SC 1407) carved out sanctuaries. " 

 16. The Supreme Court of India, in this decision, overruled some of its earlier decisions, namely, Safdarjung (AIR 1970 SC 1407), Solicitor's Case (AIR 1962 SC 1080). Gymkhana (AIR 1968 SC. 554). Delhi University (AIR 1963 SC 1873). Dhanrajiri Hospital (AIR 1975 2032) and some other rulings but upheld and approved Banerji (AIR 1953 SC 58) Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (AIR 1960 SC 610). Corporation of Nagpur (AIR 1960 SC 675). 

 17. In the Bangalore Water Supply Case the  Supreme Court glorified the decision in the case of DN Banerji vs PR Mukherjee AIR 1953 SC 58 treating it as 'the guide star' (Para-66). In the said decision Chandrasekhara Aiyar, J. while recognising the meaning of the word industry in its ordinary or non-technical sense endeavoured to give a wider meaning thus at para-10: 

 "13. having regard to the modern conditions of society where capital and labour have organised themselves into groups for the purpose of fighting their disputes and settling them on the basis of the theory that in union is strength, and collective bargaining has come to and single employee's case might develop into an industrial dispute, when as often happens, it is taken up by the trade union of which he is a member, and there is a concerted demand by the employees for redress. Such trouble may arise in a single establishment or a factory. It may well arise also in such a manner as to cover the industry as a whole in a case where the grievance, if any, passes from the region of individual complaint into a general complaint on behalf of all the workers in the industry. Such widespread extension of labour unrest is not a rare phenomenon but is of frequent occurrence. 

 From the above mentioned quotations from the Banerjj's case and the statements made in para-159 of the Bangalore Water Supply case we understand and appreciate the anxiety of the Supreme Court of India to dispense even-handed justice to the workers and to establish social justice in the said great country. No doubt, the advanced intellectual exercise shown in such a grand manner in the said case that the decision has become an example of the highest order in jurisprudence in this field and is a milestone in the legal history of this Sub-continent. Although we generally agree with their learned views, so far the workers who are employed in an industry but with greatest respect we are unable to accept it as of universal application, as for example, so far the case in hand, with regard to the employees of a city or municipal corporation, is concerned, we choose not to follow their conclusions. Out own approach is to consider the above question on the basis as to what is the dominant purpose(s) for which the concerned Corporation has been brought into existence. We shall, rather, interpret any piece of legislation as it unfolds itself in its ordinary meaning and judge it from a compassionate point of view, keeping in mind, the background for which a particular legal provision has been enacted but at the same time, it should be jealously guarded that it should not overreach it purposer We still believe, "when the meaning of words is plain it is not the duty of the Courts to busy, themselves with supposed intentions" (Lord Atkin in the case of Pakala Narayana Swami vs Emperor AIR 1939 PC 47). We still cannot ignore the warning so aptly sounded by Lord Loreburn LC in the case of Vickers Sons & Maxim Limited vs Evans 1910 AC 444: 

 We even agree with Gajendragadkar J, but with some reservations, when his Lordship held in the case of The State of Bombay vs The Hospital Mazdoor Sabha AIR 1960 SC 610: 

 But we intend to consider the said activities not in isolation but along with other attributes of social justice, for example, the reasons as to why a city corporation has been brought into existence to understand and appreciate the true import of the word 'industry'. We also agree with the views of Subba Rao, Judge in the Nagpur Corporation Case (AIR 1960 SC 675) when in considering the definition of the word 'industry' he observed at para-9, page 679: "The true meaning of the section must be gathered from the expressed intention of the Legislature". After all, the dominant question is always whether the activities of the employees of a Corporation come at all within the definition of the word 'industry' and whether they are workers in the first place. This must be decided from a compassionate point of view. Subba Rao, Judge was fully alive to the situation when he observed at para-16 in the Nagpur Corporation Case: 

 We can also visualise different situations. A particular activity of a municipality may be covered by the definition of "industry." If the financial and administrative departments are solely in charge of that activity, there can be no difficulty in treating those two departments also as part of the industry. But there may be cases where the said two departments may not only be in charge of a particular activity or service covered by the definition of "industry" but also in charge of other activity or activities falling outside the definition of "industry." In such cases a working rule may be evolved to advance social justice consistent with the principles of equity. In such cases the solution to the problem depends upon the answer to the question, whether such a department is primarily and predominantly concerned with industrial activity or incidentally connected therewith." 

 18. We are of the view that if the predominant activities of a Corporation is commercial in nature as in the case of Sonali Bank (35 DLR 151) its employees who are not in a managerial capacity, are workers but it was not so found in the case of the employees of Kumudini Hospital or the Cholera Laborator (43 DLR 655) and also in case of the employees of the Dhaka Improvement Trust (34 DLR (AD) 37). We want to consider the Labour Legislations not in isolation but in a much broader view with wider aspect, putting those legislations, not in preference but in juxtaposition to other laws of the country which are equally meant for achieving the same social justice for all citizens and not for a particular section of it. As such, of necessity, we intend to give a normal and ordinary meaning of the concerned words and not to amplify those unnecessarily, as Subba Rao, Judge himself recognised in the case of Nagpur Corporation at para-9: 

 In the case of the Ahmedabad Textile Industry s Research Association vs The State of Bombay AIR 1961 SC 484. a dispute was raised on behalf of the workmen of the Research Association, as to their wage-scale, etc before the Industrial Tribunal and an objection was raised on behalf of the Research Association as to its competency on the ground that the Research Association is not an industry within the meaning of the Act. In holding the said Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association an industry, Wanchoo, Justice held at pars-6: " 

 In this case, we are in total agreement with the conclusions reached by the learned Judge on the correct appreciation of the relevant facts. 

 20. In the case of the University of Delhi vs Ram Nath AIR 1953 SC 1873, retrenchment compensation was allowed by the Industrial Tribunal. The ground on which the challenge was made is that the work carried on by the University of Delhi is not an industry under section 2(j). Gajendragadkar, J held at para-5: 

 21. The definition of the word 'industry' was considered by the Supreme Court of India in the case of The Secretary, Madras Gymkhana Club Employees Union vs The Management of the Gymkhana Club AIR 1968 SC 554. In that case, the claim of bonus by the employees of the Club was refused by the Industrial Tribunal, Madras. The Supreme Court was primarily concerned with the question whether the club comes within the definition of 'industry' as given in the Industrial Disputes Act. Hedayetulla J, held at para-25 page-563: 

 22. In the case of Cricket Club of India vs Bombay Labour Union AIR 1969 SC 276, the question was, whether the Cricket Club of India. Bombay was an 'industry' within the meaning of section 2G) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The Club was incorporated as a company with the principal objects to encourage and promote various sports, particularly the game of cricket. It has 397 employees, at the relevant time. It had constructed 48 residential flats and 40 residential rooms. The Club owned immovable properties of the value of about Rs. 67 lac from which an income of Rs. 4 lac accrues a year. It was urged that the Club in thus constructing buildings for the purpose of earning income from rents payable by business concerns, to whom those premises are let out, is carrying on an activity which is in the nature of trade or business and, consequently it should be held that the Club is an industry, Bhargava, J held at para-l3, page-285: 

 23. In the case of The Management of Safdar lung Hospital, New Delhi vs Kuldip Singh Sethi. AIR 1970 SC 1407, raises a common question oflaw whether these hospitals can be regarded as industries within the meaning of the terms in the Industrial Disputes Act. In holding that none of the concerned hospitals are industries, Hidayatullah CJ held at para-19: 

 "We may now consider closely the Hospital Mazdoor Sabha case (1960) 2 SCR 866 == (AIR 1960 SC 610) and the reasons for which it was held that the workmen employed in a hospital were entitled to raise an industrial dispute. We may say at once that if a hospital, nursing home or dispensary is run as a business in a commercial way' there may be found elements of an industry there. Then the hospital is more than a place where persons can get treated for their ailment.' It becomes a business." 

 24. Although as a general proposition of law we agree with the views so richly propounded by the Supreme Court of India in Bangalore Water Supply Case but with great respect we prefer to follow the exposition of law with its well justified leeway (sanctuaries) in the above-noted overruled decisions. 

 25. In the instant case, a disciplinary proceeding was commenced against the respondent No.2, a market inspector, employed in the service of the Corporation and he was put under suspension on and from 31-5-1998. Enquiries were held in respect of the charges brought against him and he was found guilty in the second enquiry by the report dated 7-11-1999. Subsequently; a 'second notice to show cause was issued upon him on 11-1-2000 and he replied to the said notice on 18-1-2000. But thereafter, the Corporation neither proceeded further in the matter nor exonerated him although his order of suspension continued and he remained under suspension. Being aggrieved, the respondent NO.2 filed a case being IRO Case No. 20 of 2002 (Annexure X-17) on 10-8-2002. The petitioner- Corporation contested the said case by filling a written objection on 7-10-2002, denying all material allegations. After hearing, the Chairman of the Labour Court, declared the order of suspension of the respondent No. 2, beyond sixty-seven days, as illegal and directed payment of his full wages. The legality of the said judgment and order is under challenge in this writ petition mainly on the ground that the respondent No. 2, not being a worker, his IRO case under section 34 of the IRO was misconceived and the Labour Court acted without jurisdiction in allowing the case. 

 32. We are, however, with great respect, unable to agree with the views propounded by the Supreme Court of India in its decision in the Nagpur Corporation Case (AIR 1960 SC 675) which was upheld in the case of Bangalore Water Supply Case (AIR 1978 SC 548) that since the services of a Municipal Corporation can be rendered by an individual or a company which are industries, similarly, if those services are rendered. by a Corporation, the said Corporation would also become an industry. We are unable to agree with this view because the whole purport and context is entirely different. The dominant purpose in case of a Municipal or City Corporation is service to the community, but in the case of an individual or a company, it renders service to others for value, the dominant purpose is profit or benefit either directly or even indirectly. In the case of a Municipal or City Corporation, the people of the locality get their services themselves through their own elected representatives, employing other people within the ambit of the Ordinance. In this situation the concept of industry is totally absent which cannot be ignored in dealing with the functions of a City Corporation which is itself a creation of statute in a welfare state again, predominantly for the purpose of administering social justice in general. 

 39. A comparative study of the definition of tire said word in the Indian Act with that given in IRO would show that the words 'undertaking', 'handicraft', 'avocation of workmen' as stated in the Indian Act are absent in the IRO and the definition of the word 'industry' given in the Indian Act is, no doubt, to some extent longer but whether it is wider is open to question. This distinction, however, has also been recognised in the decision in the group of cases of Cholera Research Laboratory and another 43 DLR 655. The essential question in those cases, before the High Court, was as to whether the Cholera Research Institute is an industry within the meaning of IRO, 1969 and other related Labour Legislations. On consideration of a Nurnberg of decisions of the Supreme Court of India including the decision reported in AIR 1960 SC 610. Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J (as his Lordship then was) held at para 14: 

 40. In the instant case, the above noted distinction of the definition of the word 'industry' in the Indian Act and in the IRO, matters little since we have already held that the Chittagong City Corporation is not an industry even if it is considered in the light of the definition of the word 'industry' within the meaning of the Indian Act. The shorter definition given of the word 'industry' in the IRO, only strengthens our such view. 

 42. In the instant case, it will be convenient to refer to the relevant portion of statements made in paragraph 7 of the petition under section 34 of the IRO before the Labour Court in the IRO Case No. 20 of 2002. The said statements gave the reasons for filing the petition. It is stated therein that in accordance with the provisions of section 18(2) of the Act, a worker cannot be kept under suspension for more than 60 days and since the order of suspension dated 31-5-1998 of the first-party expired after the expiry of the said 60 days by efflux of time on 31-7-1998, he would be deemed to be present in his place of work since 31-7-1998 and is also entitled to his full emoluments. It is obvious that the first party invoked section 18(2) of the Act, claiming lifting of the order of suspension and full pay and allowance from the second party Corporation. 

 "(2) A worker charged for misconduct may be suspended pending enquiry into the charges against him and unless the matter is pending before any Court, the period of such suspension shall not exceed sixty days; 

 It is plain from the above provision that the order of suspension automatically expires by efflux of time on the expiry of60 (sixty) days from the date of the suspension. A worker is entitled to such a relief but the moot question in this case is whether the respondent No. 2 is at all a worker within the meaning of the Act. 

 43. We have examined the definitions of the words 'commercial establishment' and the 'industrial establishment' given in section 2 of the Act as quoted above. On a plain reading it is obvious that Chittagong City Corporation does not answer to the description of either the commercial establishment or industrial establishment as given in the said Act. As such, the employees of the Corporation are not workers. Reliance in this respect can be made in the decision in the case of Chairman, DITvs Chairman, Labour Court and another 34 DLR (AD) 37. 

 44. In the case of Chairman, DIT, the respondent No. 2 filed an application under section 34 of the IRO, claiming subsistence allowance and full wages. The Labour Court allowed his prayer, holding that the Dhaka Improvement Trust (the 'DIT' in short) is a commercial establishment and the respondent No. 2 was a worker within the meaning of the Act. The question before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court was as to. whether the DIT is a commercial establishment or industrial establishment and whether the respondent No. 2 was a worker, On consideration of the relevant provisions of the Act, Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J (as his Lordship then was) held at para 8: 

 Under such circumstances, the IRO case being the IRO Case No.20 of 2002, filed before the Labour Court, Chittagong, was misconceived, as such, the judgment and order dated 4-11-2002 (Annexure-A to the petition) was passed illegally and without lawful authority. 

 46. Before parting with the case, we would like to observe that section 51 of the Ordinance makes provisions for taking disciplinary actions against the employees in the Corporation including an order of suspension but no detailed rules or regulations have yet been made. 

 47. In the instant case, admittedly the, Corporation did not take any further step against the respondent No.2 on receipt of his reply dated 18-1-2000 to the second notice dated 11-1-2000. No explanation was given on behalf of the Corporation in this respect. After all, an employee cannot be kept under suspension for an indefinite period. In this case, the respondent No. 2 was put under suspension by an order dated 31-5-1998 and admittedly, his such order of suspension continued when he filed his case before the Labour Court on 10-8-2002. 

 48. Mr Nesar Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2 submits, in this connection, that he was under suspension for more than 4(four) years till he filed his IRO case and for more than 2(two) years from the date of the second notice to show-cause. This inaction .on the part of the Corporation, he submits, signifies that the Authorities of the Corporation itself did not want to depend on the perfunctory second enquiry report dated 7-11-1999 and, as such, desisted from imposing any punishment on the basis of the said enquiry report for such a long time.
